explanation.what_it_is: Iron is an essential mineral that your body uses to build hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen. It also plays roles in energy production, immune function, and DNA synthesis.
explanation.how_it_works: When you consume iron, it's absorbed in the small intestine and transported to cells throughout your body. In red blood cells, iron sits at the center of hemoglobin molecules, where it binds oxygen and transports it from your lungs to tissues. Iron also acts as a cofactor in hundreds of enzymes involved in energy metabolism, stress response, and immune signaling. Without adequate iron, your body cannot make enough healthy red blood cells or sustain normal mitochondrial function.

proven_benefits.note: Iron deficiency impairs aerobic capacity; adequate iron supports sustained physical performance and oxygen transport to muscles (26 human studies).
Iron status influences inflammatory signaling pathways; correcting deficiency or optimizing levels shows moderate benefits for inflammatory markers (7 human studies).
Iron is needed for healthy intestinal cell turnover and gut barrier integrity; adequate levels support digestion and nutrient absorption (17 human studies).
Iron is a cofactor in enzymes required for steroid hormone synthesis; deficiency impairs hormone production, and repletion can restore balance (29 human studies).
Iron supports dopamine and serotonin synthesis and helps buffer oxidative stress; deficiency is linked to anxiety, and adequate status supports mood stability (27 human studies).

explanation.emerging_research: Recent work explores iron's role in brain health and neurodegenerative disease, given its high concentration in the basal ganglia and its involvement in myelin formation. Studies are also investigating personalized iron optimization for athletic performance and recovery, and the relationship between iron status and autoimmune conditions. These areas remain early and are not yet clinical consensus.
explanation.caveats: Iron has a narrow therapeutic window—too little causes deficiency, too much can cause oxidative damage and organ harm. Iron supplementation should ideally be guided by blood tests (serum ferritin, transferrin saturation); indiscriminate supplementation in people with adequate or high iron stores can be harmful. Iron supplements may cause gastrointestinal upset, and iron from supplements is absorbed differently than food iron, so dosing and timing matter.
